● Provided equitable compensation for their work ● Provided with appropriate space ● Provided a community infrastructure, including but not limited to a cohort of others who work in the support system of the institution (CED, EEOC, Title 9, etc.) ● Job description, nomination, application and selection process. ● Job description.
The committee will develop a new job description that must convey the following critical ideas (per section 5.88.10 of the University Manual): the Ombud role shall be to: investigate complaints from students, faculty, and administrative personnel, with the very explicit charge to handle situations that fall outside of the auspices of the usual channels (such as the Office of Community, Equity, and Diversity, the unions, office of DEI in the respective colleges, EEOC, Title IX, and Human Resources).
The Ombuds are designated to handle primarily issues that stem from interpersonal conflicts. ● Application, hiring committee, and selection process.

The committee must also design a written application (whether it be an essay on qualifications and interest, or short answers to prompts) and an application and selection process that shall include a designated hiring committee.
The hiring committee shall include representatives of the university’s co-equal governing partnership: the Faculty Senate and the Office of the President.
The hiring committee shall review applications, interview candidates, and collectively make the final decision on the selection of at least two Ombuds.
It is important that there are at least two Ombuds, especially if they are full-time tenure track faculty, or faculty and staff, from two different colleges.
This allows for recusal from cases if necessary.
The SCLC recommends a two-person Office with one faculty representative and one staff representative. ● Nominations.

The Manual (5.88.11) indicates that The Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs and the Faculty Senate Executive Committee shall jointly nominate one or more full-time, tenured faculty or emeritus faculty for the post of Ombuds and shall submit the names of nominees to the Faculty Senate for confirmation, no later than May 1st of the year in which the Ombuds’ term is to begin.
Revisions must make certain that it is clear that nominations are not restricted to those put forth by any member of the administration and the Faculty Senate, but will follow the nomination and selection process designed and approved by

the special joint committee, which shall include the possibility of self-nominations. ● Visibility, privacy, and confidentiality. ● Physical space.
The committee must negotiate a new neutral space for the Office of the Ombuds that will achieve two critical goals: making the Office more visible to community members and also guarantee protections of privacy and confidentiality to those who choose to enter that space to benefit from this valuable resource. ● Communication avenues.
The committee will be charged with designing communication avenues and reporting protocols that will guarantee protections of privacy and confidentiality to those who choose to use this valuable resource. ● Digital space.
The committee will be responsible for the redesign of the Office of the Ombuds website to improve its online visibility so that the Office functions as the first stop in the reporting line.
The website must include clear messaging that is aligned with the University Manual, a more effective and reliable submission mechanism, clear expectations regarding potential courses of action and outcomes, and any other additional information that would enhance the user experience.

It would also be helpful to link the Office of the Ombuds to the other offices that handle certain student and personnel concerns, such Title IX and the CED office’s website, to increase visibility and clarity in messaging about its services.
This includes providing clear information about what the Office of the Ombuds does (and does not do).
This information is especially pertinent for new hires and newly admitted students, as well as providing ongoing messaging directed at URI employees and students. ● Reporting and Accountability.
Record keeping and reporting are critical features of a well-functioning ombud office. ● Case Reporting and Mechanisms of Accountability.
This committee must establish a policy about reporting cases, mechanisms of accountability, report storage, etc.
The reporting must not be compromised by the bureaucratic structure and must guarantee protections of privacy and confidentiality to those who choose to use this valuable resource. ● Reporting and Accountability Cohort.
The committee must create an ecosystem/cohort of other staff who are working within reporting and resolution, such as the EEOC officer, Assistant Deans

focusing on DEI, the Office of Community Equity, and Diversity, Title 9 Officer, Dean of Students, representative from HR, among others. This cohort shall meet at least twice every semester. ● Consultancy. Honors contracts are formal agreements facilitated by an honors program, between a student and instructor.
They unite students and instructors to enhance non-honors courses to an honors level through additional learner-directed work tailored to the “broader, deeper, and more complex” learning experiences advocated by the National Collegiate Honors Council (NCHC); and WHEREAS , Contracts are recognized by over 60% of honors programs in the USA, where they foster community and ownership, enhancing the educational process and commitment to the programs’ success.
For example, work at the University Honors Program at the University of Kansas shows that honors contracts act as far more than stopgaps to address honors course shortages.

They can “facilitate access to honors, increases completion, democratize key aspects of the honors experience, provide students with structured avenues for building relationships with faculty members, and empower students to own their educational experiences;” and WHEREAS , Honors contracts may be best understood as a form of an independent study, entered into voluntarily by both students and faculty, with a contract defining outcomes, deadlines, and assessment definitions for additional work related to the course materials; and WHEREAS ,Honors contracts provide flexibility for students to align their education with their interests and goals.
They also allow programs to meet student needs when constraints of students or faculty numbers or funding limitations do not allow honors courses to be run that answer to a student’s interests and needs; and WHEREAS , Contracts provide an extra measure of curricular flexibility at institutions such as ours that are not able to field enough faculty, cannot provide an adequate number of honors courses, or do not have a large enough student body to fill honors sections.

Contracts can fill the gap and provide opportunities for students’ self-guided intellectual growth; NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED , that the Faculty Senate of the University of Rhode Island, calls for implementation of the following Honors Contracts Proposal.

Overall, plan for 3-5 hours of direct faculty involvement, including evaluation.

Honors Contracts offer several beneﬁts: Flexibility: They allow students to tailor their education to their interests and goals. Accessibility: They provide opportunities for honors-level work when there are limitations on the number of honors courses offered. Student Engagement: They empower students, foster motivation, and facilitate mentor-mentee relationships with faculty. Who can supervise an Honors contract? Part-time faculty and staff may supervise contracts only in special cases if an exception is granted prior to the creation of a contract by the Honors Program. Deﬁning the terms and timeline of the contract with the student.
Providing guidance as the student works on the contracted project, with at least one mid-project meeting.
Evaluating the contract project at the end of the semester.
How much time should faculty plan to devote to this?
Generally, a faculty member should expect to devote 3-5 hours over the course of a term on a contracted project.
How are Honors Contracts set up?
The Honors Program provides comprehensive guidelines and support for setting up contracts on its Web site (See “The Contract Process”.
Students are encouraged to communicate early with instructors and the Honors Program to explore possibilities and ensure a clear understanding of the process.

What are some examples of positive outcomes from Honors Contracts?
When well-managed, Honors Contracts can: • Cultivate personalized learning experiences. • Develop strong mentoring relationships between students and faculty. • Enhance the overall honors experience. • Provide faculty with a new vision for their courses.
What are some potential problems with Honors Contracts, and how can they be avoided?
Some potential issues include: Routine or Casual Use: Contracts should not become commonplace or be considered a replacement of the regular honors curriculum.

Lack of Meaningful Interaction: Although the contracted projects require only about 20 hours of work by the student and 3 to 5 hours of work by the faculty, it is important to ensure that contracts involve meaningful interaction between students and instructors. Unclear Expectations: The Honors Program provides clear guidelines and assessment criteria to students and faculty maintain high standards. Faculty are be expected to provide clear instructions to the students in the contract language. How can I ensure that Honors Contracts are effective? To ensure effectiveness: Maintain high standards and clear expectations. Ensure that the contracted work is well-connected to the course themes and outcomes. Ensure that the contracted work enhances the student’s experience of the course themes, materials, and outcomes. Will I be compensated for my work with Honors Contracts? Yes, it is essential that faculty are recognized and compensated for the additional work involved in Honors Contracts. Your work should be noted in your review portfolio. What is the difference between an Honors contract and an Honors Project? An Honors contract deﬁnes a project requiring approximately 20 hours of work, appended to an existing non-Honors course to allow the course’s credits be counted as Honors credits. An Honors project is a mentored independent study for 3 or 6 credits, devoted to a project that requires extensive research, reading, writing, creativity, or experimentation.

BS Medical Laboratory Science, Effective Spring 2025 Appendix B The proposed change involves the addition of six courses that would qualify as "Professional Electives" towards the MLS degree.

Namely, the added courses are: BIO 331 (Parasitology), CMB 312 (Introductory Biochemistry Laboratory), CMB 332 (Medical and Public Health Microbiology Laboratory), CMB 353 (Genetics Laboratory), CMB 491 (Research in Cell and Molecular Biology), and PHP 405 (Fundamentals of Epidemiology).
The addition of these courses accomplishes two goals.
First and foremost, they provide addition al opportunities for students to cultivate lab skills in areas that are relevant to MLS (BIO 331, CMB 312, CMB 332, CMB 353 and CMB 491) as well as explore MLS-related fields (BIO 331, PHP 405) that represent potential career pathways with a MLS degree.
Second, these additional courses provide more flexibility for students to successfully complete the six credit "Professional Elective" requirement of the MLS major in a timely manner.
This is due to the fact that many of the previously approved professional electives have prerequisite course requirements and limited scheduling options (i.e. offered only during fall or spring semester), which can make it challenging for students to complete this degree requirement.
